title: Shoftim: is the tree a man? (Deuteronomy 20:19)
hook: even in war, fruit trees are spared; the rabbis made it a ban on all waste

segments.voice: Yesterday, the king who writes out the law and reads it every day. Your line was even the king reads. What line did you read before using your power? Today, a law for the middle of a war. Day five hundred five.

A city won't open its gates. The army camped outside has axes, and all around the walls stand orchards. Olive trees, fig trees, date palms that took years to grow. Cut them down, and you get timber for siege works, and you break the people inside: hungry now, and poorer for years after. In war, the usual limits tend to fall away. And right in the middle of the Torah's laws of war, there's a verse that stops an army at the edge of an orchard.
screen: `A CITY WON'T OPEN ITS GATES.` → `ORCHARDS AROUND THE WALLS.` →`AN ARMY STOPS AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the old Jewish translation: when you besiege a city a long time, "thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by wielding an axe against them." You may eat from them. You may not cut them down. And then a question: "for is the tree of the field man, that it should be besieged of thee?" The tree isn't your enemy. It can't run behind the walls. Why make it a casualty? The Hebrew can also be read as a statement: for man is a tree of the field. The medieval commentator Ibn Ezra reads it that way: people live from trees, so destroying them destroys your own life. Two readings, one point. From the words thou shalt not destroy, lo tashchit, the rabbis built a whole principle, called bal tashchit: do not destroy needlessly. And they took it far beyond orchards and far beyond war. Maimonides writes that anyone who smashes dishes, tears clothes, wrecks a building, blocks a spring or wastes food destructively breaks this law. In the Talmud, one rabbi goes further still: someone who could eat barley bread but eats the costlier wheat bread has broken it. Others there push back that caring for your own body comes first, but the reach of the idea is clear. The logic runs like this. If even in war, when everything feels permitted, you can't destroy a tree for no reason, then in peacetime, in your own kitchen, how much more. Waste isn't only careless. In this tradition, it's a kind of small destruction.
screen: `DON'T TAKE THE AXE TO THE TREES.` · `IS THE TREE A MAN?` · `BAL TASHCHIT: DON'T DESTROY.` · `IF IN WAR, HOW MUCH MORE IN PEACE.` · then, large: `DON'T DESTROY NEEDLESSLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: waste nothing today. Settle, and breathe. Picture your day in things. The food in your fridge that's close to turning. The lights left on in empty rooms. The shirt you'll throw out over one loose button. The water running while you brush your teeth. Pick three. For each, picture the small act that saves it instead. Eating the leftovers. Flipping the switch. Sewing the button. Notice that each one is tiny, and each one is a tree left standing. The bell holds the time.
Bal tashchit. Do not destroy. The rabbis' rule against needless destruction and waste, drawn from the fruit trees of Shoftim.
Your line: don't destroy needlessly. Today, save one thing you'd usually throw away: food, water, power, or something that only needs mending. Day five hundred five.

howItsDone: Bal tashchit is a recognized principle of Jewish law, applied to waste of food, objects, energy and resources, and Jewish environmental teaching often begins from this verse about the fruit trees.

fork.setup: your army is besieging a city that won't surrender. the orchards around it would make good siege timber. what does the Torah say?

eat from them, but don't cut them down.

fork.reveal: thou mayest eat of them, but thou shalt not cut them down. is the tree of the field a man, to be besieged?

original.note: Hebrew: do not destroy. the rabbis' principle against waste, from lo tashchit in Deuteronomy 20:19.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient rule about warfare.
what it means: if you can't destroy a tree for nothing even in war, then in daily life, waste is a small destruction.
what a scholar hears: Maimonides, Laws of Kings 6:10, extends it to vessels, clothes, buildings, springs and food; at Shabbat 140b Rav Chisda applies it even to choosing wheat over barley.
